question: A sports app shows live scores to 2,000,000 users and only the server produces updates. Which approach fits best?
options: Polling every second, because it is the simplest HTTP pattern
WebSockets, because every live feature needs full duplex
Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP response per client, with automatic reconnection
gRPC called directly from the browser
explanation: Traffic flows one way, so SSE gives push updates over plain HTTP, reconnects on its own and resumes with Last-Event-ID. Polling at that scale sends millions of mostly empty requests per second.

question: A site moved to HTTP/2 and pages load much faster on office Wi-Fi, but still stall on a lossy mobile network. Why?
options: All streams share one TCP connection, so one lost packet holds back every stream until it is retransmitted
HTTP/2 sends headers as plain text
HTTP/2 allows only one request per connection
Mobile networks block binary framing
explanation: HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level, but TCP still delivers bytes in order. HTTP/3 on QUIC recovers losses per stream, so a lost packet only delays the streams whose data it carried.

question: Two back-end teams want typed, fast calls between their services, including a stream of results. What do you suggest?
options: JSON over HTTP/1.1 with one connection per request
Long polling between the services
Server-Sent Events in both directions
gRPC with a Protocol Buffers schema, which generates typed clients and supports streaming over HTTP/2
explanation: gRPC generates client and server code from one schema, encodes messages in compact binary and offers server, client and bidirectional streaming on HTTP/2, which suits service-to-service calls.

question: A collaborative whiteboard sends every user's strokes to everyone else within milliseconds. What fits best?
options: Server-Sent Events, since it is plain HTTP
WebSockets: one full-duplex connection where client and server both send messages at any time
Polling every 100 ms
A gRPC unary call per stroke from the browser
explanation: Strokes flow in both directions continuously, which is the case WebSockets were built for: after the HTTP upgrade both sides send frames without a new request each time.

question: An SSE client loses its connection for a few seconds. How can the server avoid losing the events sent in between?
options: It cannot; SSE gives no way to resume
The server switches the client to WebSockets
The reconnecting EventSource sends the Last-Event-ID header, so the server replays events after that id
The browser buffers events on the server's behalf
explanation: Each event can carry an id; EventSource remembers the last one and sends it as Last-Event-ID when it reconnects, and the server resends what came after it.

question: A team adds WebSockets for chat and notices that every deploy disconnects thousands of users at once. What explains it?
options: WebSocket connections are stateful and pinned to one server, so restarting that server drops every client attached to it
WebSockets close after each message
Load balancers cannot forward the upgrade request
WebSockets only work over HTTP/3
explanation: A long-lived connection lives on one server process. Deploys need to drain connections gradually and clients need to reconnect on their own, a cost that short request-response traffic barely pays.
